# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. (b)(1) This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (2) This subdivision does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law.
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (SB 699)

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Any contract that is void under this chapter is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**. (b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (AB 1076) — notice requirement

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (b)(1) For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter, the employer shall, **by February 14, 2024, notify the employee** that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. (2) Notice shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee. (c) A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).
# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.
# Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.
# Personal jurisdiction over the employee in Texas

*Citation:* Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A forum-selection clause consenting to Travis County generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts. Two short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice; an injunction entered in Texas would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete.
# Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.

# Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP

*Citation:* 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The California Supreme Court held that §16600 voids non-competition agreements in the employment context unless they fall within a statutory exception, **rejecting the Ninth Circuit's 'narrow restraint' exception** (which had upheld restraints that barred only a small part of a profession). 'Noncompetition agreements are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions.' The court disapproved *Campbell v. Board of Trustees* and *General Commercial Packaging* to the extent inconsistent.
# Campbell v. Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University

*Citation:* 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987)  
*Status in this library:* superseded — see Edwards (2008)

Ninth Circuit applied a 'narrow restraint' exception under which a restraint barring an employee from only a small or limited part of the business, trade or profession does not violate §16600. **Status: this reasoning was rejected by the California Supreme Court in *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen* (2008); the narrow-restraint exception is not California law.**
# General Commercial Packaging, Inc. v. TPS Package Engineering, Inc.

*Citation:* 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997)  
*Status in this library:* superseded — see Edwards (2008)

Upheld a contractual provision as a 'narrow restraint' not barred by §16600. **Status: disapproved in *Edwards* (2008).**
# FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 910

*Citation:* 89 Fed. Reg. 38342 (May 7, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* vacated — see Ryan LLC v. FTC

The Rule would have declared most worker non-compete clauses an unfair method of competition and required notice to workers. **Status: set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. Aug. 20, 2024); the FTC voted in September 2025 to dismiss its appeal and accede to vacatur. The Rule never took effect and is not in force.**
# Ryan LLC v. Federal Trade Commission

*Citation:* 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The court held the FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority under §6(g) of the FTC Act to promulgate the Non-Compete Rule and that the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; it set the Rule aside with nationwide effect under the APA. The FTC's appeal to the Fifth Circuit was voluntarily dismissed in September 2025.
# Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson

*Citation:* 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The Texas Supreme Court held that a covenant not to compete in an at-will employment agreement is enforceable when the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting — **modifying *Light v. Centel Cellular* (1994)** to the extent *Light* required the consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made. The court emphasized that the core inquiry is the reasonableness of the restraint under §15.50.
# Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas

*Citation:* 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994)  
*Status in this library:* modified — see Sheshunoff (2006)

Held that a covenant not to compete must be ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement and set out a two-part test requiring that the consideration be given, and the covenant be designed to enforce the employee's return promise, **at the time the agreement is made**. **Status: the timing requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (2006); *Light* should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant.**
# Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook

*Citation:* 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Stock options granted to a managing director were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill and could support a covenant not to compete; the Court rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement for the consideration.
# DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.

*Citation:* 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Applying Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187, the Texas Supreme Court **refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause** to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy on non-competes. The case stands for the proposition that a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy.
# Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court

*Citation:* 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California follows Restatement §187: a contractual choice of law is enforced if the chosen state has a substantial relationship to the parties, unless the chosen law is contrary to a **fundamental policy** of California and California has a **materially greater interest** in the determination of the issue.
# Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.

*Citation:* 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's non-compete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; the Maryland choice-of-law clause did not control. California's policy against non-competes is 'fundamental'.
# Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic, Inc.

*Citation:* 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Addressed parallel California and Minnesota litigation over a non-compete; the Court held California courts should generally not enjoin a party from pursuing litigation in another state's courts, reversing a TRO — cautioning about interstate forum conflicts in non-compete disputes. Does not retreat from §16600's policy.
# Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc.

*Citation:* 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A rule of reason applies to §16600 challenges to restraints in **business-to-business** contracts; the Court distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void.
